newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Steady rise seen in UK Oct manuf output.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Steady rise seen in UK Oct manuf output.

text.p: Britain's manufacturing sector seems to have turned the corner and appears set to report steady growth for October, economists said on Wednesday.
But overall industrial production could be weighed down by a dip in energy output.

The Reuters consensus forecast for the figures, due on Friday at 0930 GMT, is for industrial production to have grown by 0.4 percent in October compared with September and 1.6 percent year-on-year. Manufacturing output is seen growing 0.4 percent both in the month and year-on-year.
Union Discount economist Philip Shaw said Monday's PMI (Purchasing Managers Index) data for November reflected an expansion in industry that had been restrained for months by stock overhangs.

"That pattern was reversed in the third quarter and now the trend is for manufacturing to be robust," Shaw said. The PMI index dipped to 54.4 pct in November from October's 54.5. A reading above 50.0 indicates manufacturing is expanding.
Economists at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell expect a healthy increase in October manufacturing output, similar to the 0.3 percent growth in September.
"Both the CBI and Purchasing Managers' surveys indicate that further rises in output growth lie ahead," they said.

"However, we only expect a 0.2 percent rise in overall industrial production in October as mild weather depresses energy output. Even this small rise will boost the annual rate significantly due to basis effects."

The drop in energy supply would restrict industrial output growth only to 0.3 percent, while manufacturing growth was projected at 0.5 percent month-on-month, HSBC Markets' Jonathan Loynes said. "Although September's 0.3 percent month-on-month rise left the level of manufacturing output a meagre 0.2 percent higher than a year ago, it completed a 0.7 percent increase in Q3 overall...and hence lifted manufacturing out of the technical recession in which it had floundered for the previous three quarters," Loynes said.
But September's growth was exaggerated by a rebound from a weak August figure, which would make October's growth less impressive, Salomon Brothers' economist Michael Saunders said.

"Industrial production in September benefited from higher utilities output, and we expect this factor to reverse in October, hence causing industrial production to lag manufacturing slightly," Saunders added.
Economists also warned that sterling's increasing strength could rein in further industrial growth.
"Although trade surveys have yet to suggest that the pound's rise is dampening sentiment in industry, it is hard to believe that manufacturers will escape unscathed," Loynes said.
"And a further rise, particularly if triggered by another rise in base rates, could threaten to apply the brakes to the manufacturing recovery before it gains any real momentum."

Union Discount's Shaw said interest rates could rise as soon as December 11, when Chancellor of the Exchequer (Finance Minister) Kenneth Clarke holds his monthly monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George.

"The real question is how far the strength of sterling is going to restrain export orders. If it is maintained, there's no question that it will cut the strength of the manufacturing sector," Shaw said.
